subject: ITCS217 Computer Data Communications
prompt: Which situation is NOT considered a transmission error caused by the communication channel?
explanation: A channel error changes the signal while it is on the medium. Noise, interference, and hardware faults on the path are channel errors. A mistake made by a person before the bits are sent is not caused by the channel.

sourceRefs.file: Lecture 11_ Part 1_ Attempt review _ ICT My Courses.pdf

answers: Electrical interference affects a twisted-pair cable during transmission.
Electromagnetic interference corrupts bits while they travel through a link.
Lightning produces noise near the communication transmission medium.
A user enters incorrect information into an application before transmission.
Hardware malfunction changes some signal values during transmission.
optionExplanations: Electrical interference couples into the cable while the signal is traveling, so the channel itself changes the bits. That is a transmission error.
Electromagnetic interference alters bits in transit. The damage happens on the link, so it is a channel error.
Lightning is an external noise source next to the medium. The noise is added during transmission, so the channel is the cause.
The incorrect value exists before transmission begins. The channel may then carry those bits faithfully. This is a user or application error, not a transmission error caused by the channel.
A hardware fault that changes signal values during transmission is a fault on the transmission path. It is treated as a channel error.

subject: ITCS217 Computer Data Communications
prompt: Why does an error-detection scheme add redundancy bits to the original data?
explanation: Redundancy is extra information computed from the dataword. The receiver repeats the check on the received bits and compares the result with the received redundancy. A mismatch means the data may contain errors.

sourceRefs.file: Lecture 11_ Part 1_ Attempt review _ ICT My Courses.pdf

answers: To allow the switch to assign a new MAC address to the transmitting device.
To allow the receiver to determine the application using the received data.
To allow the receiver to check whether transmitted data may contain errors.
To allow the router to determine the shortest path to the destination.
To allow the sender to increase the transmission rate of the physical link.
optionExplanations: A MAC address identifies a network interface. Error-detection bits are computed from the protected data; they do not allocate or replace addresses.
The application is identified by higher-layer information such as a port number. Redundancy bits do not name the application.

The sender adds check bits derived from the dataword. The receiver recomputes the check. Agreement supports the assumption that no error was detected; disagreement shows that the received data may be damaged.
Path selection uses routing information. A parity, checksum, or CRC field does not describe the network topology.
Adding bits increases the number of bits that must be sent for the same data, so the data throughput does not rise. The physical rate is set by the link, not by the check field.

prompt: A sender uses single even parity. The parity bit is appended to the right side of each 7-bit dataword. The datawords are 1101001, 1001000, and 1110110. Which line shows the three 8-bit codewords in that order? Formula: p = 0 when the number of 1s is even, and p = 1 when it is odd.
explanation: Even parity appends one bit on the right so each codeword has an even number of 1s. Formula: p = 0 when the dataword already has an even number of 1s, and p = 1 when that number is odd. 1101001 has four 1s, so it becomes 11010010. 1001000 has two 1s, so it becomes 10010000. 1110110 has five 1s, so it becomes 11101101.

sourceRefs.file: Lecture 11_ Part 1_ Attempt review _ ICT My Courses.pdf

optionExplanations: Formula: for even parity, p = 0 when the dataword has an even number of 1s, and p = 1 when it has an odd number. 1101001 has four 1s, so p = 0 and the codeword is 11010010. 1001000 has two 1s, so p = 0 and the codeword is 10010000. 1110110 has five 1s, so p = 1 and the codeword is 11101101.

These bits use odd parity: each codeword is forced to an odd number of 1s. 1101001 would become 11010011, 1001000 would become 10010001, and 1110110 would become 11101100. The question asks for even parity.
The parity bits 0, 0, and 1 are correct for even parity, but they were placed on the left. The question appends the parity bit on the right, so the codewords must end with those bits.
The second and third codewords are the even-parity results, but the first parity bit was flipped from 0 to 1. 11010011 has five 1s, which is odd, so the first word fails even parity.

subject: ITCS217 Computer Data Communications
prompt: A codeword protected by even parity experiences two bit errors during transmission. Which statement is most appropriate?
explanation: Even parity checks only the parity of the number of 1s. Two flips change that count by an even number, so the received word can still look even. The check then fails to report the errors, and it never identifies or repairs the two positions.

sourceRefs.file: Lecture 11_ Part 1_ Attempt review _ ICT My Courses.pdf

answers: The parity check requests retransmission before checking the codeword.
The parity check may fail because the total parity can remain even.
The parity check will always identify both erroneous bit positions.
The parity check will always correct both errors automatically.
The parity check converts the two errors into a single-bit error.
optionExplanations: The receiver evaluates the received parity first. It does not ask for a retransmission before doing that check, and a simple parity scheme has no separate request step.
Each flipped bit changes the number of 1s by one. Two flips change it by two, an even number, so an even codeword stays even. The syndrome is then zero and both errors can pass undetected.
A single parity bit has only two outcomes: the count is even or it is not. It cannot point to one position, and it cannot point to two positions.
Simple parity does not repair bits. Even a detected one-bit error needs a stronger code, such as Hamming, or a retransmission scheme.
The checker does not rewrite the received word. Two damaged bits remain two damaged bits; the check only accepts or suspects the word.

explanation: Each row gains one parity bit, and one extra parity row is sent. Formula: total = (data rows + 1) × (data bits per row + 1) = (3 + 1) × (4 + 1) = 20 bits. The same count is 12 data bits + 3 row-parity bits + 5 bits in the parity row.

subject: ITCS217 Computer Data Communications
prompt: Three 7-bit datawords are transmitted using two-dimensional even parity: 1001001, 1101100, and 0001001. Append the row parity bit to the right of each dataword and transmit the column-parity block last. Which bit stream is transmitted? Formula: p = 0 when the number of 1s is even, and p = 1 when it is odd, first for each row and then for each column including the parity column.
explanation: Append an even row-parity bit, then an even parity bit for every column, including the parity column. 1001001 has three 1s and becomes 10010011. 1101100 has four 1s and becomes 11011000. 0001001 has two 1s and becomes 00010010. The column checks then produce 01011001. The transmitted stream is 10010011 11011000 00010010 01011001.

sourceRefs.file: Lecture 11_ Part 1_ Attempt review _ ICT My Courses.pdf

optionExplanations: This is the odd-parity arrangement. 1001001 has three 1s, so odd parity appends 0; 1101100 has four 1s, so it appends 1; 0001001 has two 1s, so it appends 1. The question requires even parity, whose row bits are 1, 0, and 0.

The first three words are the correct even-parity rows, but the final block repeats the third row. The column checks are 1+1+0, 0+1+0, 0+0+0, 1+1+1, 0+1+0, 0+0+0, 1+0+1, and 1+0+0. Those counts need the parity row 01011001, not another copy of 00010010.

Row parity: 1001001 has three 1s, so append 1, giving 10010011. 1101100 has four 1s, so append 0, giving 11011000. 0001001 has two 1s, so append 0, giving 00010010. Column parity across those three rows is even, so the parity row is 01011001. The transmitted stream is 10010011 11011000 00010010 01011001.
These parity bits were inserted on the left and the column check was then taken over that layout. The required row bits stay on the right, so the first row must be 10010011 rather than 11001001.

subject: ITCS217 Computer Data Communications
prompt: The sender transmits two 8-bit words, 11010011 and 01001000. Using an 8-bit one's-complement checksum, which checksum is generated? Formula: checksum = NOT(one's-complement sum), after any carry is folded back into the 8 bits.
explanation: Formula: checksum = NOT(one's-complement sum). 11010011 + 01001000 = 100011011. Fold the carry back: 00011011 + 1 = 00011100. NOT 00011100 = 11100011.

sourceRefs.file: Lecture 11_ Part 1_ Attempt review _ ICT My Courses.pdf

optionExplanations: 00011100 is the one's-complement sum, not the checksum. 11010011 + 01001000 = 100011011. Fold the leading 1 back in: 00011011 + 1 = 00011100. The checksum is the complement of this sum.

Formula: checksum = NOT(one's-complement sum). 11010011 is 211 and 01001000 is 72, so the integer sum is 283, or 1 00011011 in 9 bits. End-around carry gives 00011011 + 1 = 00011100. NOT 00011100 = 11100011.
11100100 is the complement of 00011011. That result drops the carry out of the 8-bit sum and never adds it back. One's-complement addition must wrap that carry around before the complement.
00011011 is only the low 8 bits of 283 after the carry has been discarded. It is neither the wrapped sum nor the checksum.

subject: ITCS217 Computer Data Communications
prompt: A sender wants to transmit the hexadecimal datawords 6, C, and B using a 4-bit one's-complement checksum. Which complete binary codeword, including the checksum, is transmitted? Formula: checksum = NOT(one's-complement sum of the 4-bit words), appended after the data.
explanation: Write 6, C, and B as 0110, 1100, and 1011. Formula: checksum = NOT(one's-complement sum), appended after the data. 0110 + 1100 = 1 0010, and wrapping the carry gives 0011. 0011 + 1011 = 1110. NOT 1110 = 0001, so the codeword is 0110110010110001.

sourceRefs.file: Lecture 11_ Part 1_ Attempt review _ ICT My Courses.pdf

optionExplanations: 6, C, and B are 0110, 1100, and 1011. Add 0110 + 1100 = 1 0010, then wrap the carry: 0010 + 1 = 0011. Add 0011 + 1011 = 1110. The 4-bit checksum is NOT 1110 = 0001. The codeword is 0110 1100 1011 0001.
0110110010111110 appends 1110, which is the one's-complement sum. The transmitted check field is the complement of the sum, 0001, not the sum itself.

0110110010110010 comes from discarding the carry of 0110 + 1100 instead of wrapping it. The remaining 0010 + 1011 = 1101, and NOT 1101 = 0010. One's-complement addition has to add that carry back, producing sum 1110 and checksum 0001.
0001011011001011 places the checksum 0001 in front of the data. The question sends the datawords first and the checksum last: 0110 1100 1011 0001.
